Finite-Time Analysis of Gradient Descent for Shallow Transformers
Enes Arda Semih Cayci Atilla Eryilmaz
The Ohio State University arda.2@osu.edu RWTH Aachen University cayci@mathc.rwth-aachen.de The Ohio State University eryilmaz.2@osu.edu

Understanding why Transformers perform so well remains challenging due to their non-convex optimization landscape. In this work, we analyze a shallow Transformer with m m independent heads trained by projected gradient descent in the kernel regime. Our analysis reveals two main findings: (i) the width required for nonasymptotic guarantees scales only logarithmically with the sample size n n , and (ii) the optimization error is independent of the sequence length T T . This contrasts sharply with recurrent architectures, where the optimization error can grow exponentially with T T . The trade-off is memory: to keep the full context, the Transformer’s memory requirement grows with the sequence length. We validate our theoretical results numerically in a teacher–student setting and confirm the predicted scaling laws for Transformers.
1 INTRODUCTION

Transformers have reshaped modern machine learning, achieving state-of-the-art results in language, vision, and multi-modal tasks ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) . Despite this empirical success, a sharp nonasymptotic understanding of their training dynamics remains elusive. Two obstacles stand out: (i) the highly nonlinear nature of the self-attention layer, whereby each output coordinate depends on all inputs through a softmax reweighting, making standard arguments for fully-connected networks or CNNs difficult to apply; and (ii) the nonconvexity of the training landscape, which complicates guarantees for gradient-based methods outside of infinite-width limits.

A growing theory literature has therefore analyzed simplified settings. To make comparisons precise, let us recall the single-head self-attention layer. where σ s \sigma_{s} denotes the column-wise softmax, and β \beta is the softmax scaling. In the original Transformer, one takes β = m − 1 / 2 \beta=m^{-1/2} to stabilize the dot-product variance ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) . However, to make the analysis of ( 1 ) tractable, prior work often studies variants that take one of the following three directions: (i) avoid σ s \sigma_{s} entirely to obtain linear attention ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ; Choromanski et al., 2021 ; Lu et al., 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; (ii) replace σ s \sigma_{s} with a pointwise activation such as ReLU ( Wortsman et al., 2023 ; Hron et al., 2020 ) ; or (iii) take infinite-width limits under β = m − 1 \beta=m^{-1} , in which the softmax weights approach uniform distribution and the attention layer reduces to mean-pooling ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Noci et al., 2023 ; Bordelon et al., 2024 ) . While analytically convenient, these modifications limit the scope of the resulting guarantees.

More recently, an interesting work by Wu et al. (2023) established global convergence for shallow Transformers at finite width under the realistic β = m − 1 / 2 \beta=m^{-1/2} scaling, showing that cubic overparameterization in the sample size n n suffices for gradient descent to converge at a linear rate. Their proof follows the usual neural tangent kernel (NTK) recipe of enforcing a strict positive definiteness to a Gram matrix to drive convergence ( Du et al., 2019a ; Du et al., 2019b ; Allen-Zhu et al., 2019 ; Zou and Gu, 2019 ; Nguyen, 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ) . In particular, Wu et al. (2023) control the minimum singular value of a feature matrix built from the last hidden layer, which relies on the regime d ≥ n d\geq n , thereby limiting its practicality.

Parallel to these developments for Transformers, new techniques have sharpened finite-time analyses for recurrent architectures ( Cayci and Eryilmaz, 2024a ; Cayci and Eryilmaz, 2024b ) . Cayci and Eryilmaz (2024a) prove nonasymptotic convergence of gradient descent for IndRNNs with dramatically improved width requirements—most notably, width scaling only logarithmically in the sample size n n . Their proof is organized around norm-constrained transportation mappings that represent the target dynamical system in the RKHS induced by the RNN’s NTK, tying random-feature ideas to near-initialization training ( Rahimi and Recht, 2007 ; Ji et al., 2020 ) . Together with a projection step that keeps the gradient-descent iterates near initialization, they obtain finite-sample, finite-width convergence. The bounds also make explicit the price of long-term dependencies : beyond a cutoff governed by the activation’s Lipschitz constant, both iteration complexity and the required width can grow exponentially with the sequence length T T .

In this paper, building on techniques from Cayci and Eryilmaz (2024a) , we analyze a shallow multi-head Transformer trained by projected gradient descent algorithms ( ProjGD and ProjSGD ) in the near-initialization regime while preserving the nonlinearity of the attention layer. We address the nonlinearity and nonconvexity of the problem by working with projected updates that keep parameters in a small neighborhood of initialization. In this regime, a transportation-mapping viewpoint links the random features model induced at initialization to the NTK linearization and provides uniform control of the linearization error. We then exploit an explicit gradient characterization of the attention pathway to obtain optimization bounds independent of sequence length T T . The main contributions of this work can be highlighted as follows:

• Preserving attention nonlinearity with multiple heads. Unlike the approaches discussed above that remove or linearize softmax, or that enforce degeneracy via the scaling β = m − 1 \beta=m^{-1} , our analysis retains the genuine attention nonlinearity and allows independent heads.
• Bypassing positive definiteness of the NTK. Unlike the original works in the NTK regime, our analysis does not require strict positive definiteness of the NTK.

• Logarithmic overparameterization. We show that, in our setting, the width required for nonasymptotic training guarantees scales only logarithmically with the sample size n n . To the best of our knowledge, this has not been shown for Transformers.

• Optimization error independent of input sequence length T T . Our ProjGD bound does not degrade with the sequence length T T . This contrasts sharply with RNN analyses, where the dependence on T T can be exponential under long-term dependencies. The trade-off is memory: retaining full context implies that the Transformer’s memory footprint grows with T T due to attention over all tokens.

• Experimental validation. With controlled experiments in teacher–student settings, we validate the predicted scaling laws for our Transformer model and contrast Transformers with IndRNNs in their handling of long-term dependencies and memory complexity.
2 RELATED WORK
Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis.

The NTK framework linearizes networks around initialization and connects gradient descent to kernel gradient flow, yielding optimization and generalization guarantees in overparameterized regimes ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Du et al., 2019b ; Chizat et al., 2019 ) . For CNNs, NTK limits capture locality and weight sharing ( Garriga-Alonso et al., 2019 ; Novak et al., 2019 ) , and the convolutional NTK admits exact computation ( Arora et al., 2019 ) . For RNNs, the Recurrent NTK defines sequence kernels that aggregate contributions across time ( Alemohammad et al., 2021 ) .
Asymptotic theory for Transformers.

Representation‑theoretic results establish that Transformers are universal approximators of permutation‑equivariant sequence‑to‑sequence maps, and, with trainable positional encodings, of general continuous sequence‑to‑sequence functions on compact domains ( Yun et al., 2020 ) . At infinite width, attention admits NTK descriptions under suitable scalings: Hron et al. (2020) derive attention NTK limits, showing that under the common β = m − 1 / 2 \beta=m^{-1/2} , letting the number of heads grow results in a deterministic NTK. Under β = m − 1 \beta=m^{-1} , deterministic kernels can exist but may degenerate toward mean-pooling or require W Q = W K W_{Q}=W_{K} ( Yang, 2020 ) . Wu et al. (2023) complement their finite‑width convergence proof with an NTK analysis for shallow Transformers with β = m − 1 \beta=m^{-1} .
Nonasymptotic theory for Transformers.

Wu et al. (2023) prove global convergence of a shallow Transformer while preserving the softmax attention nonlinearity and carefully diagnosing scaling/initialization choices. Complementary results capture in‑context learning dynamics with true softmax: Huang et al. (2024) give finite‑time guarantees and a phase‑wise view of attention; Song et al. (2024) show convergence under suitable initialization and reveal that softmax can introduce spurious local minima whereas a Gaussian attention smooths the landscape. Simplified settings using linear attention establish convergence for linear predictors learned in‑context ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Beyond linear tasks, Shen et al. (2024) obtain linear‑rate convergence to the Bayes classifier for in‑context classification with a shallow multi‑head Transformer. Further optimization views sharpen what attention learns: Tarzanagh et al. (2023) show that gradient descent on a single attention layer aligns with a max‑margin (SVM‑like) token‑selection rule. Nichani et al. (2024) analyze a two‑layer attention‑only Transformer and prove that gradient descent recovers the latent causal structure of the in-context learning problem.

It can be seen that when the problem has a short-term dependency (low L L ), IndRNN achieves better results with degrading performance as L L increases; on the other hand, Transformer gives a consistent performance that does not degrade with L L , at the expense of its growing memory footprint. As such, this highlights the performance-memory trade-off between the two architectures that is anticipated by the theory.
7 CONCLUSION

We performed a finite-time NTK analysis of projected gradient methods for multi-head shallow Transformers. We established nonasymptotic convergence bounds with explicit dependencies on the training period, network width, ambient dimension, and the number of samples. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that establishes near-optimality of first-order methods without massive overparameterization for Transformers. Interesting future directions that can build on this work include the study of deep Transformer architectures and the extension of the setting to sequence-to-sequence learning.
